bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Raw material risk - availability, quality, growth and cost of sugarcane — Sugarcane is the principal raw material and is driven by factors the Company calls uncontrollable: area under cane cultivation, availability of water, adverse weather and crop disease, availability of better and higher yielding seeds, farmers shifting to other crops, diversion of cane to gur and khandsari, adequacy of harvesting and seasonal unskilled labour, un-remunerative cane procurement price, high local and state taxes, short crop cycle, fragmented land holding with low farm-level yields, mounting cane arrears and disease such as red rot. The BRSR names Raw Material Sourcing as a material risk with negative financial implications - if cane quality or quantity is affected the Company may not be able to optimally utilise its crushing capacity, directly affecting profitability. The stated mitigation is the Cane Development Programme (varietal replacement, technology adoption, farmer training), timely sourcing and timely payment to farmers, prompt clearance of cane dues, and social development measures such as schools and dispensaries in the command areas. The risk materialised this year: crush decreased as yields were affected by heavy rain / flood and unfavourable weather conditions.
- Government policy and regulatory risk - the Company operates in a price- and quantity-controlled industry — Central and State policies set the State Advised Price (SAP) and Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP) for sugarcane, control the sale of molasses, and decide both the price of sugar and the quantity of sugar a mill may sell. Mills must pay SAP to farmers irrespective of the market price of sugar. Management states plainly that these risks are Government-policy driven, beyond the Company's control and cannot be alleviated unless the industry is completely decontrolled; the response is conformity, judicial recourse where warranted, and representations through industry bodies ISMA, UPSMA and UPDA. Cost is already fixed higher for the next season - FRP for SS 2026-27 is Rs 365/qtl at 10.25% basic recovery and SAP for SS 2025-26 rose by Rs 30/qtl in both Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand - while management flags that the MSP needs to be increased from Rs 3100/qtl because the cost of production is very high compared with the MSP.
- Sugar price risk - realisation is set by markets and regulation the Company cannot influence — Domestic and international sugar prices depend on supply and demand, global prices feed directly into domestic prices, and molasses sales are controlled by the respective States. The Company states it is unable to mitigate this risk since it has no control over market forces or regulatory prices, and that the wholesale price of sugar has a significant impact on its profits. It adds that 15% to 30% of total global sugar production is traded on commodity exchanges which are speculative in nature and can adversely affect global prices and in turn its operations. Partial offsets it names are foraying into newer markets, balancing between sugar and ethanol, more value addition by concentrating on downstream projects, and improving quality.
- Cyclical risk - the sugar cycle and monsoon dependence — The industry is dependent on monsoons for both production and price realisation, and cane growers switching to other crops for better returns affects the industry. Management describes a cyclical sugar cycle in which surges in cane production crash market prices and pile up stocks, while shortages send raw material costs soaring and cause factory sickness. The Company again states it is unable to mitigate this risk, relying instead on Government irrigation initiatives, augmentation of canal irrigation and tapping of available water surpluses.
- Climate change risk - identified as material with no mitigation measures in place — The BRSR material-issues table records Climate Risk as a risk with negative implications, noting that climate change can adversely impact the business and that not having a correct strategy or its right implementation will severely affect business continuity - and states explicitly that the Company does not have any mitigation measures to tackle climate-change-related risk, relying only on ensuring the production process is not hampered and that production and delivery remain timely. This sits alongside the separately identified risk of the effect of climate change on agricultural produce and the cyclic nature of the sugar industry.
- Water risk and environmental compliance liability — Water is identified in the BRSR as a finite resource that poses a risk to operations, with negative financial implications; mitigations cited are measures to reduce water consumption in sugar manufacturing, operating sugar units with zero ground water extraction, and rainwater harvesting systems feeding the manufacturing process. Separately, the MD&A flags environmental regulatory risk - the industry and the Company are subject to environmental regulations and may be exposed to liability from handling hazardous materials and to potential costs for environmental compliance - with zero ground water extraction in the sugar plants and zero liquid discharge in the distillery cited as measures taken.
- Finance risk - dependence on timely working capital and long-term funding — The MD&A identifies the industry's dependence on the availability of timely working capital at competitive interest rates, and on long-term finance for capacity enhancements, economic size of mills and manufacture of by-products. The mitigation paragraph is cut off in this bundle, so the Company's stated response to this risk cannot be reported.
- Concentration risk - a single cane-based value chain in two adjacent states, and an unresolved State Government loan flagged by the auditor — All output - sugar, co-generated power, industrial alcohol and ethanol - derives from one agricultural input in one geography: of the four sugar manufacturing units, three are located in Uttar Pradesh and one in Uttarakhand, which the BRSR argues are places where cane-sourcing risk is minimum but which also concentrates weather, policy (SAP) and crop-disease exposure in two adjoining states. On the accounting side, the auditor's Emphasis of Matter draws attention to note no. 37(c) on the unsecured loan of Rs 656.68 Lakhs received as one-time assistance from the State Government of Uttarakhand in January 2008: no demand has ever been raised, a waiver application for the outstanding loan and interest has been filed with the appropriate authority, and pending the final outcome the Company has not accounted for interest on the loan after 31.03.2024, aggregating Rs 52.52 lakh up to the year ended 31st March 2026. The auditor's opinion is not modified in respect of this matter.

outlook.body: This bundle discloses no named company capex or expansion project, no commissioning or ramp timeline and no rupee capex quantum. outlook.body:
- Sugar realisation was the swing factor in the year: EBITDA was higher mainly on account of better sales realisation of sugar and improvement in distillery production and sugar recovery, partly offset by the Rs 30/qtl increase in cane SAP and lower crush from crop damage caused by excessive rains and floods
- Cane availability is weather-exposed - the decrease in crush is attributed to yield affected by heavy rain / flood and unfavourable weather conditions; nationally, sugar production has moderated on lower cane availability and increasing diversion of sugar to ethanol
- Domestic sugar demand is described as relatively inelastic, with average consumption around 280 lakh tonnes, providing predictable demand for sugar producers even as production fluctuates
- Indian sugar output in 2026/27 is forecast to recover 3.6 million metric tons (raw value) to 33.6 million as consecutive monsoons restored groundwater reserves and improved yields, with area planted and harvested forecast at nearly 6.0 million hectares, a 2 percent increase
- Exports have declined sharply on government restrictions; the Government of India prohibited sugar exports with effect from 13th May 2026 in view of lower sugar stock, and closing stock is estimated around 4.25 million MT at the end of sugar season 2025-26 - the projected closing stock of 42.5 lakh tonnes in 2025-26 is described as being at a marginal level
- Cane cost is set by policy and is rising: SAP for UP and Uttarakhand rose Rs 30/qtl for SS 2025-26 to Rs 400 and Rs 405 per quintal for early variety, and FRP for SS 2026-27 is fixed at Rs 365/qtl for a basic recovery of 10.25%, with a Rs 3.56/qtl premium or reduction per 0.1% change in recovery
- Management flags that the MSP of sugar needs Government intervention and should be increased from Rs 3100/qtl, as the cost of production is very high compared with the MSP
- Ethanol is the structural growth engine but is entering an overcapacity phase: India's ethanol capacity has scaled to about 2000 crore litres with an additional 400 crore litres expected operational by FY27, against E20 fuel demand of only about 1100 crore litres and non-fuel demand of about 300-350 crore litres, with only about 60% of offered ethanol being absorbed
- The ethanol sector is transitioning into a consolidation phase, with utilisation levels likely to remain in the ~65-75% range for the next three years, EPC activity moderating and industry focus shifting toward brownfield capex, debottlenecking and operational efficiencies; about 700 crore litres of excess supply relative to absorption is expected to keep margins under pressure in the near to medium term
- Ethanol capacity is regionally concentrated - surpluses in Maharashtra (277 crore litres) and deficits such as 77 crore litres in Tamil Nadu - creating dependence on long-distance transportation, higher logistics costs and pressure on realisations
- Meaningful ethanol demand expansion depends on higher blends (E85/E100) and Flex Fuel Vehicle adoption; MoRTH's draft amendments released on April 27, 2026 point toward E85 or exclusive ethanol fuel, and excise duty exemption has been extended to E22, E25, E27 and E30 with BIS notification of those grades expected to improve demand further
- E85 rollout has begun at 48 fuel pumps run by state-owned oil marketing companies, initially in the national capital region including New Delhi and Mumbai, Pune and Nagpur, with the petroleum and natural gas ministry stating it would be scaled up to 500 fuel stations by December 2026 and about 5,000 fuel outlets by December 2027
- Ethanol feedstock mix has shifted to grain: in the ESY 2025-26 tender allocation, total grain accounted for 763 crore litres (72%) against 290 crore litres (28%) from sugarcane out of 1053 crore litres contracted, so enough quantity is available for the ethanol requirement
- Ethanol infrastructure remains a constraint - a single-grade retail network of about 1.03 lakh outlets, storage capacity of about 77.8 crore litres and reliance on 300+ centralised depots - adequate for E20 rollout but not aligned with multi-blend requirements
- Blending has already reached about 20%: an average 20% ethanol blending level was reached in December 2025, five years ahead of schedule, and as of April 30, 2026 around 514 crore litres of ethanol had been supplied to OMCs with blending of 19.99% achieved
- Co-generation output tracks cane crush - power production and export decreased mainly due to lower cane crush, with surplus power sold to UPPCL/UPCL

risks.risk: Raw material risk - availability, quality, growth and cost of sugarcane
risks.note: Sugarcane is the principal raw material and is driven by factors the Company calls uncontrollable: area under cane cultivation, availability of water, adverse weather and crop disease, availability of better and higher yielding seeds, farmers shifting to other crops, diversion of cane to gur and khandsari, adequacy of harvesting and seasonal unskilled labour, un-remunerative cane procurement price, high local and state taxes, short crop cycle, fragmented land holding with low farm-level yields, mounting cane arrears and disease such as red rot. The BRSR names Raw Material Sourcing as a material risk with negative financial implications - if cane quality or quantity is affected the Company may not be able to optimally utilise its crushing capacity, directly affecting profitability. The stated mitigation is the Cane Development Programme (varietal replacement, technology adoption, farmer training), timely sourcing and timely payment to farmers, prompt clearance of cane dues, and social development measures such as schools and dispensaries in the command areas. The risk materialised this year: crush decreased as yields were affected by heavy rain / flood and unfavourable weather conditions.

risks.risk: Government policy and regulatory risk - the Company operates in a price- and quantity-controlled industry
risks.note: Central and State policies set the State Advised Price (SAP) and Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP) for sugarcane, control the sale of molasses, and decide both the price of sugar and the quantity of sugar a mill may sell. Mills must pay SAP to farmers irrespective of the market price of sugar. Management states plainly that these risks are Government-policy driven, beyond the Company's control and cannot be alleviated unless the industry is completely decontrolled; the response is conformity, judicial recourse where warranted, and representations through industry bodies ISMA, UPSMA and UPDA. Cost is already fixed higher for the next season - FRP for SS 2026-27 is Rs 365/qtl at 10.25% basic recovery and SAP for SS 2025-26 rose by Rs 30/qtl in both Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand - while management flags that the MSP needs to be increased from Rs 3100/qtl because the cost of production is very high compared with the MSP.

risks.risk: Sugar price risk - realisation is set by markets and regulation the Company cannot influence
risks.note: Domestic and international sugar prices depend on supply and demand, global prices feed directly into domestic prices, and molasses sales are controlled by the respective States. The Company states it is unable to mitigate this risk since it has no control over market forces or regulatory prices, and that the wholesale price of sugar has a significant impact on its profits. It adds that 15% to 30% of total global sugar production is traded on commodity exchanges which are speculative in nature and can adversely affect global prices and in turn its operations. Partial offsets it names are foraying into newer markets, balancing between sugar and ethanol, more value addition by concentrating on downstream projects, and improving quality.

risks.risk: Cyclical risk - the sugar cycle and monsoon dependence
risks.note: The industry is dependent on monsoons for both production and price realisation, and cane growers switching to other crops for better returns affects the industry. demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Sugar realisation was the swing factor in the year: EBITDA was higher mainly on account of better sales realisation of sugar and improvement in distillery production and sugar recovery, partly offset by the Rs 30/qtl increase in cane SAP and lower crush from crop damage caused by excessive rains and floods
- Cane availability is weather-exposed - the decrease in crush is attributed to yield affected by heavy rain / flood and unfavourable weather conditions; nationally, sugar production has moderated on lower cane availability and increasing diversion of sugar to ethanol
- Domestic sugar demand is described as relatively inelastic, with average consumption around 280 lakh tonnes, providing predictable demand for sugar producers even as production fluctuates
- Indian sugar output in 2026/27 is forecast to recover 3.6 million metric tons (raw value) to 33.6 million as consecutive monsoons restored groundwater reserves and improved yields, with area planted and harvested forecast at nearly 6.0 million hectares, a 2 percent increase
- Exports have declined sharply on government restrictions; the Government of India prohibited sugar exports with effect from 13th May 2026 in view of lower sugar stock, and closing stock is estimated around 4.25 million MT at the end of sugar season 2025-26 - the projected closing stock of 42.5 lakh tonnes in 2025-26 is described as being at a marginal level
- Cane cost is set by policy and is rising: SAP for UP and Uttarakhand rose Rs 30/qtl for SS 2025-26 to Rs 400 and Rs 405 per quintal for early variety, and FRP for SS 2026-27 is fixed at Rs 365/qtl for a basic recovery of 10.25%, with a Rs 3.56/qtl premium or reduction per 0.1% change in recovery
- Management flags that the MSP of sugar needs Government intervention and should be increased from Rs 3100/qtl, as the cost of production is very high compared with the MSP
- Ethanol is the structural growth engine but is entering an overcapacity phase: India's ethanol capacity has scaled to about 2000 crore litres with an additional 400 crore litres expected operational by FY27, against E20 fuel demand of only about 1100 crore litres and non-fuel demand of about 300-350 crore litres, with only about 60% of offered ethanol being absorbed
- The ethanol sector is transitioning into a consolidation phase, with utilisation levels likely to remain in the ~65-75% range for the next three years, EPC activity moderating and industry focus shifting toward brownfield capex, debottlenecking and operational efficiencies; about 700 crore litres of excess supply relative to absorption is expected to keep margins under pressure in the near to medium term
- Ethanol capacity is regionally concentrated - surpluses in Maharashtra (277 crore litres) and deficits such as 77 crore litres in Tamil Nadu - creating dependence on long-distance transportation, higher logistics costs and pressure on realisations
- Meaningful ethanol demand expansion depends on higher blends (E85/E100) and Flex Fuel Vehicle adoption; MoRTH's draft amendments released on April 27, 2026 point toward E85 or exclusive ethanol fuel, and excise duty exemption has been extended to E22, E25, E27 and E30 with BIS notification of those grades expected to improve demand further
- E85 rollout has begun at 48 fuel pumps run by state-owned oil marketing companies, initially in the national capital region including New Delhi and Mumbai, Pune and Nagpur, with the petroleum and natural gas ministry stating it would be scaled up to 500 fuel stations by December 2026 and about 5,000 fuel outlets by December 2027
- Ethanol feedstock mix has shifted to grain: in the ESY 2025-26 tender allocation, total grain accounted for 763 crore litres (72%) against 290 crore litres (28%) from sugarcane out of 1053 crore litres contracted, so enough quantity is available for the ethanol requirement
- Ethanol infrastructure remains a constraint - a single-grade retail network of about 1.03 lakh outlets, storage capacity of about 77.8 crore litres and reliance on 300+ centralised depots - adequate for E20 rollout but not aligned with multi-blend requirements
- Blending has already reached about 20%: an average 20% ethanol blending level was reached in December 2025, five years ahead of schedule, and as of April 30, 2026 around 514 crore litres of ethanol had been supplied to OMCs with blending of 19.99% achieved
- Co-generation output tracks cane crush - power production and export decreased mainly due to lower cane crush, with surplus power sold to UPPCL/UPCL

capital_allocation.title: Strategy & capital allocation
capital_allocation.body:
- Strengthen cane development to protect cane availability and recovery - developing an in-house agri research centre, running an integrated pest management programme, providing soil testing facilities, encouraging bio-fertilizer use, installing a laboratory and bio-pesticides, and running training facilities for farmers and cane development staff
- Run the distilleries on the richer feedstock route where possible - the three UP units operated on B-heavy molasses, Barkatpur additionally on syrup with B-heavy molasses and Libberheri on B-heavy and C-heavy molasses - with distillery capacity about 25% higher than the C-heavy basis when a plant operates on B-heavy molasses or syrup
- Scale distillery throughput and the ethanol stream, with alcohol production rising to 877 lakh BL in FY 2025-26 from 666 lakh BL in FY 2024-25, an increase of 32% over the previous year
- Grow the branded and specialty sugar business - continuous focus on sachet, icing, invert and cubes (white and brown) - and widen presence across General Trade, Modern Trade, HORECA and corporate customers, with new major HORECA buyers such as IRCTC, CCD, Starbucks, Mother Dairy, Flipkart, Blinkit and Zepto

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: This bundle discloses no named company capex or expansion project, no commissioning or ramp timeline and no rupee capex quantum. What it does state on capacity is the existing footprint: the Company has two distilleries with an installed capacity of 300 KLPD, of which 250 KLPD is at Barkatpur, stated on the basis of working on C-heavy molasses; where a plant operates on B-heavy molasses or syrup the capacity will be further higher by 25%. Existing distillery capacity was worked harder rather than added to during the year - alcohol production rose to 877 lakh BL in FY 2025-26 from 666 lakh BL in FY 2024-25, an increase of 32%, with the three UP units operating on B-heavy molasses, Barkatpur also on syrup with B-heavy molasses and Libberheri on B-heavy and C-heavy molasses. The only capability build described is on the cane side, where the Company is strengthening cane development through development of an in-house agri research centre, an integrated pest management programme, soil testing facilities, installation of a laboratory and bio-pesticides and farmer training facilities. At industry level, management notes that with ethanol capacity of about 2000 crore litres plus an upcoming 400 crore litres against demand of about 1100 crore litres for fuel and about 350 crore litres for non-fuel uses, EPC activity has begun to moderate and industry focus is shifting toward brownfield capex, debottlenecking and operational efficiencies - but the Company states no expansion plan of its own here. The Capital Commitments notes (Note No. 24 at page 94 and Note No. 23 at page 128) and the segment Capital Expenditure disclosures (pages 97 and 131) appear in this bundle as headings only, carrying no attributable figure.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Full forward integration of the cane stream: sugar, bagasse-based co-generation and molasses/syrup-based distillery operate off one cane intake, so by-products of sugar manufacture become saleable power, industrial alcohol, ethanol and potash
- Assured institutional offtake across all three streams - Power Purchase Agreements with UPPCL and Uttarakhand Power Corporation Limited for surplus power, and supply of ethanol to public Oil Marketing Companies under the Ethanol Blended Petrol programme
- Flexibility of the distillery to run on B-heavy molasses, C-heavy molasses or syrup, with capacity about 25% higher when operating on B-heavy molasses / syrup rather than C-heavy
- Improving cane recovery: net sugar recovery was 9.42% in SS 2025-26 against 8.94% in SS 2024-25 with B-heavy molasses/syrup, and recovery equivalent to C-heavy molasses was 11.35% against 11.28%
- In-house cane development capability - an in-house agri research centre under development, an integrated pest management programme, soil testing facilities, promotion of bio-fertilizer, an installed laboratory and bio-pesticides, and training facilities for farmers and cane development staff
- A branded and specialty sugar franchise (sachet, icing, invert, cubes in white and brown) showing continuous growth, with widening presence across General Trade, Modern Trade and HORECA and named new buyers such as IRCTC, CCD, Starbucks, Mother Dairy, Flipkart, Blinkit and Zepto
- Wide product ladder within sugar - sulphur-less refined, double refined, natural brown, liquid, pharma, icing, sachet, cubes and candy - supporting realisations beyond bulk sugar; net sales realisation of sugar was better at Rs 4143 per qtl in the current year against Rs 3984 per qtl in the previous year

risks.title: Bear — key risks
risks.body:
- Raw material risk - availability, quality, growth and cost of sugarcane — Sugarcane is the principal raw material and is driven by factors the Company calls uncontrollable: area under cane cultivation, availability of water, adverse weather and crop disease, availability of better and higher yielding seeds, farmers shifting to other crops, diversion of cane to gur and khandsari, adequacy of harvesting and seasonal unskilled labour, un-remunerative cane procurement price, high local and state taxes, short crop cycle, fragmented land holding with low farm-level yields, mounting cane arrears and disease such as red rot. The BRSR names Raw Material Sourcing as a material risk with negative financial implications - if cane quality or quantity is affected the Company may not be able to optimally utilise its crushing capacity, directly affecting profitability. The stated mitigation is the Cane Development Programme (varietal replacement, technology adoption, farmer training), timely sourcing and timely payment to farmers, prompt clearance of cane dues, and social development measures such as schools and dispensaries in the command areas. The risk materialised this year: crush decreased as yields were affected by heavy rain / flood and unfavourable weather conditions.
- Government policy and regulatory risk - the Company operates in a price- and quantity-controlled industry — Central and State policies set the State Advised Price (SAP) and Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP) for sugarcane, control the sale of molasses, and decide both the price of sugar and the quantity of sugar a mill may sell. Mills must pay SAP to farmers irrespective of the market price of sugar. Management states plainly that these risks are Government-policy driven, beyond the Company's control and cannot be alleviated unless the industry is completely decontrolled; the response is conformity, judicial recourse where warranted, and representations through industry bodies ISMA, UPSMA and UPDA. Cost is already fixed higher for the next season - FRP for SS 2026-27 is Rs 365/qtl at 10.25% basic recovery and SAP for SS 2025-26 rose by Rs 30/qtl in both Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand - while management flags that the MSP needs to be increased from Rs 3100/qtl because the cost of production is very high compared with the MSP.
- Sugar price risk - realisation is set by markets and regulation the Company cannot influence — Domestic and international sugar prices depend on supply and demand, global prices feed directly into domestic prices, and molasses sales are controlled by the respective States. The Company states it is unable to mitigate this risk since it has no control over market forces or regulatory prices, and that the wholesale price of sugar has a significant impact on its profits. It adds that 15% to 30% of total global sugar production is traded on commodity exchanges which are speculative in nature and can adversely affect global prices and in turn its operations. Partial offsets it names are foraying into newer markets, balancing between sugar and ethanol, more value addition by concentrating on downstream projects, and improving quality.
- Cyclical risk - the sugar cycle and monsoon dependence — The industry is dependent on monsoons for both production and price realisation, and cane growers switching to other crops for better returns affects the industry. Management describes a cyclical sugar cycle in which surges in cane production crash market prices and pile up stocks, while shortages send raw material costs soaring and cause factory sickness. The Company again states it is unable to mitigate this risk, relying instead on Government irrigation initiatives, augmentation of canal irrigation and tapping of available water surpluses.
- Climate change risk - identified as material with no mitigation measures in place — The BRSR material-issues table records Climate Risk as a risk with negative implications, noting that climate change can adversely impact the business and that not having a correct strategy or its right implementation will severely affect business continuity - and states explicitly that the Company does not have any mitigation measures to tackle climate-change-related risk, relying only on ensuring the production process is not hampered and that production and delivery remain timely. This sits alongside the separately identified risk of the effect of climate change on agricultural produce and the cyclic nature of the sugar industry.
- Water risk and environmental compliance liability — Water is identified in the BRSR as a finite resource that poses a risk to operations, with negative financial implications; mitigations cited are measures to reduce water consumption in sugar manufacturing, operating sugar units with zero ground water extraction, and rainwater harvesting systems feeding the manufacturing process. Separately, the MD&A flags environmental regulatory risk - the industry and the Company are subject to environmental regulations and may be exposed to liability from handling hazardous materials and to potential costs for environmental compliance - with zero ground water extraction in the sugar plants and zero liquid discharge in the distillery cited as measures taken.
- Finance risk - dependence on timely working capital and long-term funding — The MD&A identifies the industry's dependence on the availability of timely working capital at competitive interest rates, and on long-term finance for capacity enhancements, economic size of mills and manufacture of by-products. The mitigation paragraph is cut off in this bundle, so the Company's stated response to this risk cannot be reported.
- Concentration risk - a single cane-based value chain in two adjacent states, and an unresolved State Government loan flagged by the auditor — All output - sugar, co-generated power, industrial alcohol and ethanol - derives from one agricultural input in one geography: of the four sugar manufacturing units, three are located in Uttar Pradesh and one in Uttarakhand, which the BRSR argues are places where cane-sourcing risk is minimum but which also concentrates weather, policy (SAP) and crop-disease exposure in two adjoining states. On the accounting side, the auditor's Emphasis of Matter draws attention to note no. 37(c) on the unsecured loan of Rs 656.68 Lakhs received as one-time assistance from the State Government of Uttarakhand in January 2008: no demand has ever been raised, a waiver application for the outstanding loan and interest has been filed with the appropriate authority, and pending the final outcome the Company has not accounted for interest on the loan after 31.03.2024, aggregating Rs 52.52 lakh up to the year ended 31st March 2026. The auditor's opinion is not modified in respect of this matter.
